supplement.where: Additional files 1 and 2 at https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00631-0 (p. 19, Supplementary Information). Neither is appended to or embedded in the supplied PDF, and neither was found among matching local files. At finalization, Python urllib requests to the DOI and https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40594-026-00631-0 both failed with socket-permission error WinError 10013; no supplementary contents were retrieved.
supplement.holds: According to the main text: Additional file 1 contains the final problem posing Tests 1 and 2 (p. 9); Additional file 2 contains baseline between-group tests, within-group pre/post tests, and ENA baseline and within-group visualizations (p. 13). Exact supplementary statistics were not available for verification. Post-test between-group means, SDs, Ns, t, df, p, and Cohen's d are printed in Table 5 on p. 13.

paper_design_summary: Two third-grade classes at one school in central China were randomized at the class level to a custom GLM-4 chatbot or Baidu search during three science inquiry lessons; 97 students were randomized by class and 89 were analyzed with complete pre/post test data (pp. 5-6, 12). Researchers scored the questions students generated on number, category, cognitive quality, and a total problem-posing score, and compared category/quality networks from tests and tool-assisted classroom records (pp. 10-14). The reported random allocation during ordinary coursework supports field_rct despite the paper's quasi-experimental label; post-test tool availability, timing, and the underlying ENA analysis units are not explicitly reported.

studies.label: Class-randomized comparison of GLM-4 chatbot and Baidu search for science question generation

assignment.what_was_assigned: Chatbot versus search-engine condition, allocated to two intact classes by randomly selecting one as the experimental class and using the other as control; one class per arm.
assignment.quote: One class was randomly selected as the experimental group (N = 48), and the other as the control group (N = 49), with technology conditions allocated at the class level.
assignment.locator: p. 5, Methods, Participants; p. 1, Abstract. Classification follows the reported random allocation in ordinary coursework, despite the authors' quasi-experimental label.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration is stated in the supplied full text.

arms.name: Experimental group (chatbot)
arms.description: Question Pot, a researcher-configured chatbot on the ChatGLM platform using GLM-4, accessed on tablets for multi-round dialogue during the science inquiry lessons; 48 students randomized by class and 45 analyzed with complete pre/post tests (pp. 5-6, 8, 12-13).

arms.name: Control group (search engine)
arms.description: Baidu keyword-based search and reading on tablets during the same inquiry lessons; 49 students randomized by class and 44 analyzed with complete pre/post tests (pp. 5-6, 8, 12-13).

participants.exclusions: The study collected 185 test papers. Baseline analysis used 90 analyzed students (46 chatbot, 44 search). Post-test and longitudinal analyses required complete pre- and post-test participation: 89 students were analyzed from the 97 randomized by class, comprising 45 of 48 chatbot students and 44 of 49 search-engine students. The paper does not give a separate test-exclusion count or individual reasons for missing test participation; the reported allocation and analysis counts are retained without inferring those reasons. Of 93 questionnaires, 7 were excluded for missing data or straightlining, and 86 respondents were analyzed (42 chatbot, 44 search). A separate instrument pilot involved 30 students explicitly outside the study sample (p. 5, Participants and Implementation procedure; p. 12, Data analysis; p. 13, Table 5).
participants.who: Third-grade students aged 8-9 in two classes at one primary school (p. 5, Participants).
participants.quote: The final number of valid samples included in the analyses was 89 (45 in the experimental group and 44 in the control group).
participants.locator: p. 5, Participants (97 assigned, 48/49); p. 12, Data analysis (89 complete cases, 45/44); p. 13, Table 5.

ai_tool.name_model: Question Pot, a custom chatbot on the ChatGLM platform using GLM-4 (p. 8, Technology-based scaffolds).
ai_tool.how_used: Students used multi-round natural-language dialogue to generate and refine questions during inquiry lessons (p. 6). The custom prompts guided questioning, question chains, and cross-disciplinary thinking; example questions were available in all three topics. Follow-up suggestions were available only in Topic 1 and then disabled to discourage copying; the Smart Star motivational mechanism was added in Topics 2-3 (p. 8, Table 2). This is interactive chat that can supply content, so it does not meet the codebook's content-free coach definition. The paper describes tablet access during the inquiry lessons but does not explicitly document removal or prohibition of tools during the tests.

task.description: Generate or reformulate open-ended scientific questions from contextual prompts. Each test contained three items (two text-only, one text plus image); Test 2 concerned wind formation, compression of air, and applications of air in daily life. Students supplied questions, not answers. In-lesson questions were generated and developed through the assigned tool during three thematic inquiry topics (pp. 4, 6-9).
task.duration: 15 minutes per formal test (pp. 8-9). Three thematic inquiry topics, each with regular lessons and one problem-based inquiry lesson (p. 6). Total intervention length and elapsed time between the final lesson and post-test are not stated.

outcomes.name: Post-test total problem posing ability score (maximum 10)
outcomes.measure_detail: Total of number, category, and quality scores, with maximum contributions of 3, 2, and 5 points (p. 11, Eq. 1 and scoring paragraph). Two trained researchers coded questions, resolving disagreements by discussion; pilot kappa = 0.886 (p. 11), and kappa = 0.827 on 20% of formal data (p. 12). This is a problem-posing composite, not a direct overall-creativity rating. No primary endpoint hierarchy is explicitly designated.
outcomes.delay: Not stated. The post-test follows the inquiry phase (p. 6, Fig. 1), but neither a separate later session nor a same-session immediate test is established. The elapsed interval and whether tools were available during testing are unreported; after_ai is therefore not confirmed.

contrasts.reported: Total Score: experimental M 5.80 (SD 0.59, N = 45) vs control M 5.36 (SD 0.73, N = 44); t = 3.07, df = 82.61 (adjusted), p = 0.003, Cohen's d = 0.65
contrasts.locator: p. 13, Table 5 (including the footnote on adjusted degrees of freedom).

outcomes.name: Post-test question quality score (Bloom cognitive level)
outcomes.measure_detail: Question codes use remembering/understanding R = 1, applying P = 2, analyzing A = 3, evaluating E = 4, and creating C = 5 (p. 10, Table 3). Eq. 4 is the mean of these point values over a student's valid questions; the stated maximum contribution is 5 (p. 11). A 0-5 range or an additional rescaling step is not stated. The paper says the rubric considers complexity, novelty, and uniqueness, but it measures depth of cognitive processing rather than a separate novelty or overall-creativity score (pp. 10-11). No primary designation for this subscore is stated.
outcomes.delay: Not stated. The post-test follows the inquiry phase (p. 6, Fig. 1), but neither a separate later session nor a same-session immediate test is established. The elapsed interval and whether tools were available during testing are unreported; after_ai is therefore not confirmed.

outcomes.name: Post-test question number score (banded count)
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of interrogative questions per student, excluding declarative statements; Table 3 gives L1 <= 5, L2 = 6-10, L3 = 11-15, L4 = 16-20, L5 >= 20, and Eq. 2 gives S_number = L x 0.6, maximum 3 (pp. 10-11). The reported outcome is the banded score, not a raw question count. The printed L4 and L5 thresholds overlap at 20; the intended handling of that boundary is not specified.
outcomes.delay: Not stated. The post-test follows the inquiry phase (p. 6, Fig. 1), but neither a separate later session nor a same-session immediate test is established. The elapsed interval and whether tools were available during testing are unreported; after_ai is therefore not confirmed.

outcomes.name: Post-test question category score (weighted type score)
outcomes.measure_detail: Table 3 assigns IQ irrelevant = 0, SC context-based = 1, SL learned knowledge = 2, SR real-life = 3, OD other-discipline = 1, and CQ comprehensive = 2 (p. 10). Eq. 3 is (2/3) times the mean category point value over valid questions, with maximum contribution 2 (p. 11). This is not a count of distinct categories and therefore is not flexibility. The explanatory prose below the equations instead says an irrelevant question receives 1 point, contradicting Table 3; both statements are retained as a source inconsistency rather than silently resolving the implemented weight.
outcomes.delay: Not stated. The post-test follows the inquiry phase (p. 6, Fig. 1), but neither a separate later session nor a same-session immediate test is established. The elapsed interval and whether tools were available during testing are unreported; after_ai is therefore not confirmed.

outcomes.name: Post-test epistemic network structure (category x quality code co-occurrence)
outcomes.measure_detail: ENA of researcher-coded question category and cognitive quality, retaining 11 codes and presenting group mean and subtracted networks (p. 12, Data analysis; p. 13, Results RQ2; p. 14, Fig. 3). The observation and accumulation/stanza units used to construct the mean networks are not stated; unit is null because a displayed group mean does not establish the analysis unit. Visual description only; no inferential network contrast or numerical effect is reported. Co-occurrence of codes is not similarity across different people, so this is not diversity.
outcomes.delay: Not stated. The post-test follows the inquiry phase (p. 6, Fig. 1), but neither a separate later session nor a same-session immediate test is established. The elapsed interval and whether tools were available during testing are unreported; after_ai is therefore not confirmed.

contrasts.reported: Descriptive only: the chatbot group had stronger connections around SL, SR, P, and E; the search group had stronger connections around R, including R-SC and R-P (p. 13). Neither group formed stable connections involving the creating node at any stage (p. 17). No inferential network statistic is reported.

outcomes.name: In-lesson epistemic network structure across inquiry Topics 1-3
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: ENA of category and cognitive-quality codes from Question Pot dialogue records and Baidu search records while students used their assigned tools (pp. 6, 12). Group mean networks and centroid trajectories are shown across Topics 1-3 (p. 14, Fig. 4). The number dimension was not coded and no problem-posing ability scores were calculated for this phase (p. 11). The observation and accumulation/stanza units used to construct the mean networks, and the per-phase participant counts, are not stated; unit and n_units remain null. These are code co-occurrences, not across-person output-similarity estimates.

contrasts.reported: No statistics. Experimental network expanded and deepened across topics with more nodes participating; control network showed localized changes in connection strength with node count unchanged.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is met by explicit random allocation of two classes to a generative-AI chatbot or Baidu search during ordinary coursework (p. 5, Participants; pp. 6, 8, intervention and tool descriptions), supporting field_rct. Criterion 2 is met by 89 analyzed students, 45 chatbot and 44 search, rather than the repeated test papers or coded questions (p. 12, Data analysis; p. 13, Table 5). Criterion 3 is met by researcher-scored open-ended questions: the number score measures fluency, and the cognitive-quality rubric considers novelty and uniqueness and includes generating new ideas or original designs (pp. 8, 10-12; Table 3). The broader problem-posing and ENA outcomes retain construct other. Correcting the two ENA analysis units to null does not affect the verified participant-level output scores. Post-test tool availability and timing remain unknown, affecting with_ai versus after_ai classification and timing rather than these eligibility criteria. One randomized class per arm and participant-level t-tests provide no reported class-adjusted precision; the printed precision is not eligible for pooling as though clustering were accounted for (pp. 5, 12-13; codebook section 10).

one_line_finding: After the inquiry lessons, the chatbot class had higher total problem-posing scores (5.80 vs 5.36; p = 0.003; d = 0.65) and question-quality scores (2.46 vs 2.29; p = 0.015; d = 0.52), with no significant number or category differences (p. 13, Table 5).
open_questions: Were AI and search tools removed or prohibited while students produced the post-test questions? The paper-test format and sequence alone do not confirm this, so S1-O1 through S1-O5 have null question and AI-availability fields pending explicit administration instructions.
Was the post-test in the same session or a later session, and how much time elapsed after the last inquiry lesson? Timing is null for S1-O1 through S1-O5.
Was any output outcome prospectively designated primary? No preregistration or explicit endpoint hierarchy is reported in the supplied paper; all primary fields are not_stated.

Additional files 1 and 2 remain unavailable: finalizer requests to the DOI and Springer article page were blocked by socket permissions. The main text identifies the test instruments in Additional file 1 (p. 9) and baseline/within-group statistics and ENA visualizations in Additional file 2 (p. 13); their exact contents remain unverified.
What observation, accumulation, and stanza units were used for the post-test ENA mean networks in S1-O5? Group means and a subtracted network do not identify the underlying analysis unit (pp. 12-14).
What observation, accumulation, and stanza units, and how many analyzed participants per topic, were used for the inquiry-phase ENA in S1-O6? These are not stated (pp. 12-14).
How were exactly 20 questions assigned to number-score bands? Table 3 includes 20 in both L4 and L5 (p. 10).
What point value was actually used for irrelevant questions in the category score? Table 3 gives IQ = 0, but the explanatory prose gives 1 (pp. 10-11).
notes: Both raw forms parsed successfully. The entire 817-line markdown conversion was read, including references and supplementary-material notices; the 22-page PDF has no appended supplementary files. Relevant PDF pages, Table 5 via text-based table extraction, Fig. 1, and the displayed scoring equations were checked. The raw forms list the same six output outcomes, with the same constructs, measures, units, comparison type, and four numerical post-test contrasts. Differences in wording or inclusion of equivalent locators are not counted. Outcome timing disagreements are counted separately for each of the five affected outcomes; the repeated disagreement about post-test tool availability in the one-line finding, AI-use description, and caveats is counted once. No primary endpoint hierarchy is explicitly stated; not_stated is used for all six outcomes, also correcting the raw forms' agreed primary/secondary labels. The null question, availability, and timing fields are deliberate unknowns under the brief's no-guessing rule; the provided categorical vocabulary has no unknown option for these fields. No post-test outcome is classified as none, because its question is unknown rather than irrelevant. There is only one randomized class per condition (p. 5). The paper uses independent-sample student-level t-tests (p. 12; Table 5, p. 13), with adjusted degrees of freedom for category and total score but no reported class-level correction. Printed effect sizes are retained without recalculation; reported precision should not be pooled as though class randomization had been accounted for. The pilot is a separate instrument check, not an additional AI-comparison study (p. 5). Baseline and within-group tests are summarized in the main text, with detailed statistics in Additional file 2 (p. 13); no inaccessible numerical results are reconstructed. The 3010 coded entries combine phases and are not people or an outcome-specific n_units (p. 12). Self-reported cognitive load and technology acceptance are excluded from the output outcomes. For completeness, B's additional numbers were verified: overall cognitive-load score M = 4.59 versus 4.17, t = 2.41, p = 0.018, and overall technology acceptance M = 5.27 versus 4.75, t = 3.09, p = 0.003; questionnaire N = 86 (42/44) (pp. 12, 14-15; Fig. 5 on p. 15 and Fig. 6 on p. 16). Higher scores indicate lower load and higher acceptance. Table 3 overlaps the number bands at 20 questions and gives irrelevant questions 0 points, whereas the explanatory prose on p. 11 says 1 point; these are source inconsistencies, not silently repaired scoring rules. Neither group had stable creating-node connections (p. 17), so the positive quality effect is not represented as evidence of increased highest-level creativity. Reconciliation counts refer to substantive differences between A and B; agreed fields corrected by source checking are also documented below. Finalization: all 817 markdown lines, including supplementary notices and references, were reread. The PDF assignment, participant accounting, rubric, equations, Table 5, and network figures were independently checked. Both challenged ENA unit fields are now null; the reconciliation object is preserved as a historical record. Every original open question and all seven unresolved reconciliation differences are covered by final.open_items, with duplicated timing questions grouped explicitly. None affects the three eligibility criteria. Final n_corrected/n_rejected/n_open count challenge dispositions only; an unsupported field can be corrected to null while the underlying missing detail remains an open item.

a.finding: On a paper post-test taken after three inquiry lessons, the chatbot class outscored the search-engine class on total problem posing ability (5.80 vs 5.36, t = 3.07, p = 0.003, d = 0.65) and question quality (2.46 vs 2.29, p = 0.015), with no significant difference in number or category (p. 13, Table 5).
a.caveat: The paper does not state explicitly that tablets and tools were unavailable during the post-test; coding as after_ai rests on the post-test being a separate 15-minute paper test (stage 5 in Fig. 1, '185 test papers', researcher monitoring).

b.finding: On a paper post-test taken without AI, third-graders whose class used a GenAI chatbot during inquiry lessons scored higher than the search-engine class on total problem posing ability (5.80 vs 5.36, t = 3.07, p = 0.003, d = 0.65) and question quality (2.46 vs 2.29, p = 0.015, d = 0.52), with no significant differences in number or category (p. 13, Table 5).

open_items.item: Post-test AI/search access for S1-O1 through S1-O5 (open_questions[0] and the unresolved reconciliation difference on post-test AI availability): explicit administration rules would settle with_ai versus after_ai. Both classifications preserve the three eligibility criteria.

Post-test session and elapsed interval for S1-O1, S1-O2, S1-O3, S1-O4, and S1-O5 (open_questions[1] and all five unresolved reconciliation timing differences, studies[0].outcomes[0] through studies[0].outcomes[4]): a dated administration schedule would settle immediate versus delayed timing; eligibility does not depend on that distinction.

Prospective outcome priority (open_questions[2] and unresolved reconciliation difference studies[0].outcomes[1].primary): an existing dated protocol or preregistration supplied by the authors would establish any primary designation. This affects primary-record selection, not eligibility.

Uninspected Additional files 1 and 2 (open_questions[3]): obtain the test instruments and detailed baseline/within-group analyses and ENA visualizations identified on pp. 9, 13, and 19. The main text already establishes random assignment, the analyzed-person count, and output scoring.

Underlying ENA observation and accumulation/stanza units for S1-O5 (open_questions[4]; corrected outcome challenge): the authors' ENA specification or project export would identify them. The participant-level score outcomes independently satisfy the output criterion.

Underlying ENA observation and accumulation/stanza units and analyzed participant counts per inquiry topic for S1-O6 (open_questions[5]; corrected outcome challenge): an author-provided ENA specification and sample accounting would settle these fields. The verified 89-person post-test analysis and scored outputs establish eligibility independently.

Number-score boundary at exactly 20 questions (open_questions[6]): the implemented scoring rule or author clarification would resolve the overlapping L4/L5 thresholds in Table 3. This affects score reconstruction, not whether questions were scored or the eligibility criteria.

Implemented IQ category point value (open_questions[7]): the scoring code or author clarification would resolve Table 3's 0 versus the explanatory prose's 1. This affects score reconstruction, not the eligibility criteria.
